messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 61
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Sculptor
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 41

**Vignette: Mei-Lin, 61-year-old married sculptor**

---

Mei-Lin is sixty-one years old, a woman whose hands have spent decades shaping clay and stone into forms she describes as "what the world cannot say out loud." She grew up in a coastal city in Vietnam and emigrated with her husband to the United States in her early thirties. For most of her adult life, she has carried herself with a quiet steadiness — the kind that people mistake for serenity but that she knows, privately, is simply the discipline of keeping busy.

Three years ago, Mei-Lin was visiting her younger sister's neighborhood when she witnessed a man struck by a vehicle at an intersection near a street market. The driver did not stop. Mei-Lin ran toward him and knelt beside him on the pavement. She held his hand and spoke to him softly while waiting for an ambulance, watching his breathing become shallow and then stop before help arrived. She did not know him. She has never learned his name. That absence — the anonymity of his death, the fact that he left the world without anyone who loved him present — is something she returns to constantly, though she does not want to.

In the weeks following, Mei-Lin told herself she was fine. She cleaned her studio, accepted a commission for a memorial piece, cooked elaborate meals for her husband on weekends. But sleep began to leave her. She would lie in the dark and see the man's face — not as it looked in those final moments, but as she imagines it looked that morning when he woke up, before he knew. She cannot explain why her mind does this. She only knows it will not stop.

She began avoiding the street market entirely, and then the broader neighborhood, rerouting her drives across the city in ways that add twenty minutes to ordinary errands. Her husband noticed but said little at first, attributing it to her introverted nature. She did not correct him. When he eventually asked, she told him she was tired, which was true, though not in the way she meant it.

Her work has changed in ways that disturb her. She used to sculpt figures in motion — dancers, children, birds mid-flight. Now she finds herself drawn to heaviness. She has produced three large pieces in the past two years that her gallery describes as "meditative" and "confronting mortality with grace." She accepts the praise but knows the work is not graceful. It is frightened. She is frightened, and the clay is the only place she can put it.

She startles easily now — at car horns, at the sudden movement of someone stepping off a curb nearby. At a farmer's market last spring, a display table collapsed with a loud crack, and Mei-Lin found herself crouched against a wall before she understood what had happened. A stranger asked if she was all right. She said yes and walked to her car and sat there for forty minutes before she could drive.

She feels a persistent low-grade guilt that she finds both irrational and immovable. She wonders whether she should have done something differently, spoken different words to him, whether her presence comforted him or whether she was simply a stranger watching him die. She does not speak of this to her husband, who she describes as a kind man but one who believes that suffering should be "moved through." She loves him. She also feels very alone.

Some evenings she sits in her studio after the light has gone and does not turn on the lamps. She is not sure what she is waiting for in those moments. She says it is the only time her mind goes quiet — not peaceful, but quiet, which is the closest she can get.
